chunks.title: Debt service ratio and responsible lending
chunks.section: What the debt service ratio measures
chunks.content: The debt service ratio (DSR) compares a borrower's monthly debt repayments with their monthly income. It answers a simple question: of every ringgit that reaches the borrower each month, how much is already promised to lenders? Banks in Malaysia are expected under Bank Negara Malaysia's responsible lending guidance to assess whether a borrower can repay without undue hardship, and the DSR is the main measure they use to do it.

chunks.title: Debt service ratio and responsible lending
chunks.content:
Banks compute the DSR on net income: the salary after statutory deductions. Those deductions are the employee EPF contribution, SOCSO, EIS and monthly tax deductions (PCB). A buyer who quotes their gross salary will always overstate what the bank counts.

Variable income such as commission, overtime and bonuses is treated cautiously. Many lenders discount it or average it over a long period because it may not recur. LifeNest AI applies a haircut to variable income before computing net income; the size of the haircut is set in the versioned rules file.

chunks.title: Debt service ratio and responsible lending
chunks.content: Every existing monthly repayment is added to the numerator: car loans, personal loans, study loans, other housing loans, and credit card obligations. The new housing loan instalment is then added on top. A car loan taken out a year before applying for a mortgage can reduce the property price a buyer can reach by much more than the car itself cost, because each ringgit of monthly commitment removes many ringgit of borrowing capacity over a long tenure.

chunks.title: Debt service ratio and responsible lending
chunks.content: Each bank sets its own internal DSR limits, and they are not published as a single national rule. Limits commonly rise with income, because a higher-income household has more left over after essential spending. LifeNest AI uses an indicative banded table: up to 60% for net income up to RM3,000 a month, 65% up to RM5,000, 70% up to RM10,000, and 75% above that. These bands are configuration, not law, and a particular bank may apply stricter or more generous limits.

chunks.title: Debt service ratio and responsible lending
chunks.section: Why self-declared budgets diverge from computed capacity
chunks.content:
Buyers often set a budget from a figure they can comfortably imagine paying each month, or from a property they have already seen. Neither starts from net income and existing commitments. The result is a budget that can sit far above what any bank would lend, and buyers discover this only after paying for a booking, a valuation or legal advice.

LifeNest AI starts from the other end. It computes the DSR from the confirmed payslip and commitments, works out the monthly instalment the DSR still allows, and converts that instalment into a maximum loan and price using the configured rate and tenure. The `compute_dsr` tool reports net income, total commitments, the DSR, the applicable band and the monthly headroom. The `loan_capacity` tool then reports the maximum loan and price and names the factor that limits them.

A DSR inside the band does not mean a loan will be approved. Banks also consider credit history, employment stability, the property itself and their own risk appetite.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: EPF Akaun Sejahtera and housing withdrawals
chunks.content:
In May 2024 the Employees Provident Fund (EPF, or KWSP) restructured every member's savings into three accounts. Akaun Persaraan holds the retirement savings and receives 75% of each monthly contribution. Akaun Sejahtera receives 15% and supports life-cycle needs such as housing, education and health. Akaun Fleksibel receives 10% and can be withdrawn for any purpose.

Before the restructure, members had two accounts. The former Account 1 received 70% of contributions and the former Account 2 received 30%. Housing withdrawals were drawn from Account 2.

chunks.title: EPF Akaun Sejahtera and housing withdrawals
chunks.section: Where housing withdrawals come from now
chunks.content:
Under the 2024 structure, housing withdrawals draw on Akaun Sejahtera. Because Akaun Sejahtera receives 15% of contributions where the former Account 2 received 30%, a member's housing pot now grows at roughly half the old pace for the same salary. The balances that existed in Account 2 at the time of the restructure were carried across, but every contribution since then splits under the new shares.

LifeNest AI reads the Akaun Sejahtera balance from the member's EPF statement and treats that balance as the amount available for a housing withdrawal. It does not count Akaun Persaraan, and it does not count Akaun Fleksibel towards the housing withdrawal, because the fleksibel balance is not reserved for housing and may already be committed elsewhere.

chunks.title: EPF Akaun Sejahtera and housing withdrawals
chunks.section: What a housing withdrawal may be used for
chunks.content:
EPF housing withdrawals are generally available to help buy or build a house, to reduce or settle an outstanding housing loan, and to help pay monthly housing loan instalments. Eligibility depends on conditions such as the property type, the relationship of the member to the property owner, and how often the member has already withdrawn for housing. The exact withdrawal limit for a purchase is set by KWSP and is capped by the Akaun Sejahtera balance.

Withdrawals for a purchase are usually paid against the difference between the purchase price and the financing, so they help with the down payment. Many of the other upfront costs, such as stamp duty and legal fees, still need to be paid in cash.

chunks.title: EPF Akaun Sejahtera and housing withdrawals
chunks.section: Why pre-2024 numbers overestimate the down payment
chunks.content:
Many buyers still plan with figures from articles, calculators or family advice written before May 2024. Those sources assume 30% of contributions flow into the housing account. A buyer who projects their housing pot forward on that basis will expect roughly twice the monthly growth they will actually see.

The effect compounds. A buyer planning to wait two or three years to build a down payment from EPF alone may find the pot is far smaller than expected on the day they sign. That gap then has to come from cash savings, which pushes the purchase date back or reduces the price they can safely commit to.

chunks.title: EPF Akaun Sejahtera and housing withdrawals
chunks.content:
The `epf_withdrawal` tool returns the Akaun Sejahtera balance, the amount LifeNest treats as eligible, and a note about the 2024 structure. The upfront-cost calculation subtracts that eligible amount from the total cash needed and shows any shortfall that must come from savings. Future EPF contributions are not assumed in any plan, so the plan is never optimistic about EPF.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: First-home assistance and guarantee schemes
chunks.content: Many first-time buyers can afford the monthly instalment on a modest home but cannot assemble the down payment and upfront costs. Others have irregular income that a bank finds hard to verify. Malaysian federal and state governments, together with banks and government-linked agencies, run schemes aimed at these gaps. Their names, terms and funding change over time, so this note describes the common types rather than the current terms of any particular scheme.

chunks.title: First-home assistance and guarantee schemes
chunks.content:
**Credit guarantee schemes.** A government-backed guarantor covers part of the loan, which lets a bank lend more than it otherwise would. This can raise the margin of finance above the usual level and reduce the down payment a buyer needs. Some guarantee schemes are aimed at buyers without a fixed monthly salary, such as gig workers and small traders.

**Stamp duty exemptions.** First-time buyers may receive full or partial exemption from stamp duty on the memorandum of transfer and the loan agreement, up to a price ceiling and within a set period.

**Affordable housing programmes.** Federal and state programmes offer homes at controlled prices to eligible buyers, often with resale restrictions for a period after purchase.

**Developer and bank packages.** Some developers absorb legal fees or offer rebates, and some banks offer special first-home financing. These are commercial offers, and their true value should be compared with a standard loan.

chunks.title: First-home assistance and guarantee schemes
chunks.content:
Most schemes test some combination of the following:

- **First-property status.** The buyer, and sometimes their spouse, must not already own residential property.
- **Household income ceiling.** Combined monthly household income must fall below a stated limit.
- **Property price ceiling.** The property must cost no more than a stated limit.
- **Citizenship and age.** Applicants are usually Malaysian citizens within an age range.
- **Property type and use.** The home must be residential and owner-occupied.

chunks.title: First-home assistance and guarantee schemes
chunks.content:
A scheme can change what a buyer can afford, sometimes significantly. Because terms change and eligibility depends on details only the scheme operator can confirm, LifeNest AI does not apply any scheme automatically in its calculations. Its figures assume a standard loan with no exemptions or guarantees. A buyer who may qualify should check current terms with the relevant ministry, agency or bank, and then compare the result with LifeNest's standard figure.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.content: The tenure is the number of years over which a housing loan is repaid. Malaysian banks commonly offer housing loans of up to 35 years. LifeNest AI uses 35 years as the maximum in its indicative rules.

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.section: The cap by age at maturity
chunks.content:
Banks also limit how old a borrower may be when the loan ends. A common cap is 70 years old at maturity, although some banks use a lower age and a few allow a higher one. LifeNest AI uses 70.

The tenure a buyer can actually get is the shorter of the two limits. A 29-year-old can take the full 35 years, because they would be 64 at maturity. A 40-year-old is capped at 30 years. A 60-year-old is capped at 10 years. Someone already at the age limit cannot take a new housing loan on their own.

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.section: How a shorter tenure changes the numbers
chunks.content:
The monthly instalment on a loan depends on the amount, the interest rate and the tenure. Shortening the tenure spreads the same principal over fewer payments, so each payment rises. Because the debt service ratio caps the instalment a buyer can afford, a shorter tenure also lowers the loan the buyer can reach.

The effect is strong at long tenures and becomes severe at short ones. Losing five years from a 35-year tenure trims capacity noticeably. Losing twenty years cuts it by more than half.

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.section: Choosing a shorter tenure on purpose
chunks.content: Some buyers choose a shorter tenure to pay less interest overall. That is a reasonable goal, but it means a higher instalment and a lower maximum price. LifeNest AI lets the buyer ask for a specific tenure, and `loan_capacity` will use the shorter of the requested tenure and the age-based cap.

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.content: Banks often allow an older borrower to extend the tenure by applying jointly with a younger co-borrower, sometimes using the younger borrower's age for the cap. Those arrangements depend on the bank and on both borrowers' circumstances, and LifeNest AI does not model them. Its calculation uses the age on the confirmed profile.

chunks.title: Loan tenure and the age cap at maturity
chunks.content:
The `loan_capacity` tool computes the tenure as the minimum of the configured maximum, any tenure the buyer requested, and the years left before the age cap. When the age cap is what shortens the tenure, the tool reports `TENURE_AGE` as the limiting factor so the buyer understands why their capacity is lower than a younger buyer's on the same income.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: Margin of finance for housing loans
chunks.content:
The margin of finance is the share of the property price a bank is willing to lend. If the margin is 90%, the bank lends up to 90% of the price (or of the valuation, if lower) and the buyer funds the remaining 10% as a down payment. The margin is sometimes called the loan-to-value ratio.

The margin sets the minimum down payment, so it directly shapes the cash a buyer needs on the day of purchase. A lower margin means a larger down payment for the same property.

chunks.title: Margin of finance for housing loans
chunks.content: For a buyer's first and second housing loans, Malaysian banks commonly offer a margin of up to 90%. LifeNest AI uses 90% for both in its indicative rules. Some government-backed or bank-specific first-home programmes can offer a higher margin, but those depend on the scheme's eligibility conditions and are not assumed in the calculation.

chunks.title: Margin of finance for housing loans
chunks.content:
Bank Negara Malaysia introduced a maximum margin of 70% for a borrower's third and subsequent outstanding housing loans. The aim was to cool speculative buying and keep household debt sustainable. LifeNest AI applies 70% whenever the confirmed profile shows two or more existing housing loans.

At 70%, the buyer must fund 30% of the price in cash, three times the down payment on a 90% loan. Stamp duty and other costs come on top. In practice this cash requirement, rather than income, is usually what limits a third purchase.

chunks.title: Margin of finance for housing loans
chunks.section: What counts as a prior housing loan
chunks.content:
A prior housing loan generally means any outstanding loan or financing facility secured on residential property in the borrower's name, including joint loans. A loan that has been fully settled usually no longer counts. Banks check the borrower's credit report to identify existing housing facilities, so a buyer cannot avoid the tighter margin by leaving a loan off their application.

Loans taken on commercial property, or personal loans used for renovation, are typically treated differently, but each bank applies its own definitions.

chunks.title: Margin of finance for housing loans
chunks.content:
The margin is chosen from the number of existing housing loans in the confirmed profile. The `loan_capacity` tool converts the maximum loan into a maximum property price by dividing by the margin. The `upfront_costs` tool uses the same margin to compute the down payment and the loan amount on which loan stamp duty is charged. When a reduced margin is what makes the cash requirement bind, LifeNest reports the limiting factor as `MARGIN_OF_FINANCE` so the buyer can see the reason.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: Standardised Base Rate and housing loan pricing
chunks.content: The Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) is the interest rate set by Bank Negara Malaysia's Monetary Policy Committee. It is the main tool the central bank uses to steer borrowing costs across the economy. Changes to the OPR are announced after scheduled committee meetings.

chunks.title: Standardised Base Rate and housing loan pricing
chunks.content:
Since 1 August 2022, new retail floating-rate loans in Malaysia reference the Standardised Base Rate (SBR). The SBR is tied to the OPR: when the OPR moves, the SBR moves by the same amount, and it changes for no other reason. This makes it easy for borrowers to see that a change in their loan rate came from monetary policy rather than from a bank's own decision.

Older loans may still reference a bank's Base Rate or Base Lending Rate, which can also move for bank-specific reasons.

chunks.title: Standardised Base Rate and housing loan pricing
chunks.section: The spread and the effective rate
chunks.content:
A floating-rate housing loan is priced as the reference rate plus a spread. The spread reflects the bank's view of the borrower and the loan, its funding costs and its profit margin. The spread is fixed in the loan agreement, although some loans step the spread up after an initial period.

The effective lending rate is the reference rate plus the spread. In its indicative rules LifeNest AI takes the OPR as the reference, because the SBR tracks it exactly, and adds a standard-applicant spread of 1.65 percentage points. With the OPR at 2.75% that gives an effective rate of 4.40%. A stronger applicant may obtain a narrower spread, but LifeNest uses the standard spread so that its figures are not optimistic.

chunks.title: Standardised Base Rate and housing loan pricing
chunks.section: What happens when the OPR moves
chunks.content:
When the OPR rises, the SBR rises with it, and so does the effective rate on every floating-rate loan that references it. The bank then either raises the monthly instalment or keeps it the same and extends the time needed to repay, depending on the loan terms. On a long-tenure loan, a one-percentage-point rise can add a meaningful amount to each instalment.

For a buyer who has borrowed close to their DSR limit, that increase comes straight out of their monthly buffer.

chunks.title: Standardised Base Rate and housing loan pricing
chunks.content:
All rates live in one versioned rules file. Changing the OPR is a single-line edit, and every calculation then uses the new effective rate. The `loan_capacity` tool reports the effective rate it used. The `rate_rise` scenario in `simulate_scenario` adds a configured increase to the rate from a chosen month, recomputes the instalment on the outstanding balance, and shows whether the household's cashflow still holds.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.section: Stamp duty on the memorandum of transfer
chunks.content:
When ownership of a property passes to the buyer, the memorandum of transfer (MOT) is stamped and duty is charged on the property price or market value, whichever is higher. The duty is tiered, and each rate applies only to the slice of the price that falls inside its tier:

- 1% on the first RM100,000
- 2% on the portion from RM100,001 to RM500,000
- 3% on the portion from RM500,001 to RM1,000,000
- 4% on the portion above RM1,000,000

On a RM500,000 property the MOT duty is therefore RM1,000 plus RM8,000, a total of RM9,000.

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.section: Stamp duty on the loan agreement
chunks.content:
The loan or financing agreement is also stamped, at 0.5% of the loan amount. On a loan of RM450,000 that is RM2,250.

First-time buyers may qualify for full or partial exemptions on both duties under government first-home initiatives, subject to a price ceiling and a deadline. LifeNest AI does not apply any exemption automatically, because eligibility must be confirmed by the buyer's lawyer. Its figures are therefore the cost before any exemption.

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.content: Lawyers are paid for the sale and purchase agreement and for the loan documentation, and their fees follow a regulated scale that is tiered by price. LifeNest AI uses an indicative tiered scale on the property price: 1.25% on the first RM500,000, 1.00% on the portion up to RM1,000,000, and 0.70% above that. Actual quotations vary with the transaction and may be charged separately for the purchase and the loan.

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.content: The bank requires a valuation report, and its fee is roughly proportional to the property value. LifeNest uses 0.25% of the price as an indicative valuation cost. Disbursements cover searches, registration, courier, printing and similar out-of-pocket items; LifeNest uses a flat RM1,500.

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.content: The housing loan finances only part of the price, up to the margin of finance. Everything else is paid upfront: the down payment, both stamp duties, legal fees, valuation and disbursements. Some banks allow certain fees to be added to the loan, but this is not assumed. An EPF housing withdrawal can help with the down payment, but the remaining costs usually need cash.

chunks.title: Stamp duty, legal fees and other upfront costs
chunks.content:
The `upfront_costs` tool returns each of these items for a given price, the total cash needed, the eligible EPF amount applied against it, and the shortfall after EPF. If the buyer has declared savings, the shortfall after savings is shown too. When cash runs out before the DSR does, `loan_capacity` reports `CASH_UPFRONT` as the limiting factor.

*Indicative guidance. Verify current terms with the relevant authority. Not a lending decision.*
